answers.java_tx_design: In ClaimsCore, our claims-adjudication service, I once had a transaction that updated a claim's status and then, inside the same @Transactional method, called out to a notification service to email the policyholder. During our nightly batch settlement run, when a few thousand claims move status at once, that external call held the transaction open long enough that other threads updating the same claims table piled up -- I saw over 90 threads blocked on row locks in one run, which pushed batch runtime from 40 minutes to almost two hours. I moved the notification call out of the transaction entirely: the status update commits on its own, and I write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction, which a separate poller picks up to send the email. Batch runtime dropped back under 45 minutes. The failure I didn't foresee at first: the poller could double-send an email if it crashed after sending but before marking the outbox row done, so I added a sent_at check before resending.
answers.java_ops: On the same service, we had connection pool exhaustion during month-end reinsurance reporting, when a reporting job ran alongside normal traffic. HikariCP wait time spiked to about 800ms at p95, and normal claim submissions started timing out. I pulled thread dumps during the next occurrence and found the reporting job was holding connections open for the full length of a multi-minute aggregation query instead of releasing them between steps. I rewrote the job to commit and release its connection after each chunk of about 5,000 claims instead of holding one connection for the whole run, and moved it onto a separate 8-connection pool so it couldn't compete with live traffic at all. p95 wait time on the main pool dropped back under 20ms during the next month-end run.
answers.rust_readiness: I don't have production Rust experience. What I have is a couple of personal projects -- the more serious one is a small tool that ingests our claims export CSVs and cross-checks totals, which I rewrote in Rust over a few weekends to force myself past tutorials. I hit real ownership and lifetime problems doing that, which I can go into detail on. My honest view on migrating something like ClaimsCore: I wouldn't propose a full-service rewrite, I'd want to find one boundary that's stateless and easy to verify by comparing outputs against the existing Java path, run both for a while, and only trust the new one once the outputs matched for a sustained period. That's closer to how I'd want to treat any Rust adoption here, given I'm still building real experience rather than claiming production depth I don't have.
answers.rust_boundary: For a ledger-like write path I don't have a production example, but for my claims-CSV tool I did have to decide a boundary of sorts: I kept CSV parsing and validation in Rust, since that's where the tool spends most of its time and where compiler-checked correctness helps most, but I left the eventual write into our reporting database as a separate Python script I already trusted, rather than pulling database access into the Rust side too. What I'd watch in a real production boundary: latency and error rate on the new path, and a running count of any output mismatches against the old path -- the same comparison approach I used to convince myself my Rust totals matched what the old spreadsheet-based process produced before I trusted it.
answers.money_correctness: In ClaimsCore, claim payment submissions to our payment processor carry an idempotency key built from claim_id plus a payment attempt sequence number, stored with a unique constraint in a payment_attempts table. About two years ago, a processor-side timeout caused our retry logic to resend a batch of 60 payment requests with a bug in how the sequence number incremented, so 60 requests reused a sequence number that had already succeeded, and our unique constraint silently rejected the retries as duplicates -- which sounds safe, except six of those claims had genuinely different amounts because of a same-day adjustment, and the retries got dropped instead of processed. I found it during weekly reconciliation when six claims showed as paid in our system but the processor showed no matching transaction. I corrected those six manually with new payment entries, not edits to the rejected ones, and fixed the sequence-number bug so it's tied to payment content, not just an incrementing counter.
answers.incident_response: Around the same period, we had an incident where our adjudication engine's state machine let a claim move from 'approved' straight to 'paid' without passing through a required fraud-review step, for about 45 minutes before I caught it via a mismatch alert on our review-queue depth. Four claims went through that path, totaling around $31,000. I flagged it in our incident channel within ten minutes of noticing, before I'd even confirmed the root cause, paused the affected transition, and had a fix -- a missing state-guard condition -- deployed within two hours. All four claims went through manual fraud review after the fact, and none were found fraudulent, but we still treated it as the process failure it was. The postmortem added an automated test that asserts every terminal state transition passes through its required guard, and I wrote that test myself.
answers.process_skipping: Yes, and I'll be honest about it rather than give the tidy answer. During the state-machine incident I just described, I deployed the guard-condition fix myself about ninety minutes in, without waiting for a second reviewer, because claims were actively bypassing fraud review while I waited. I posted in the incident channel right before deploying, not after, saying I was skipping review given active harm, and I logged the diff afterward for the team to review once things were calm. Looking back, I think I could have gotten a one-line ack from anyone online in under two minutes before pushing rather than announcing and going -- the situation didn't actually require skipping that check, just doing it fast, and I've tried to hold myself to a stricter bar since. It's the one time I've done it, and I don't think it was as necessary as it felt in the moment.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing a mistake: I once shipped a change to claim-amount rounding that was subtly wrong for a specific currency path, and I found it myself two days later while checking something unrelated. I posted about it in our team channel that same afternoon, tagged my manager, and we quantified the impact -- 14 claims, all under $3 difference -- before I'd been asked anything. On-call: I've carried our claims-platform rotation for four years, one week in five, and it's genuinely part of how I think about the job, not separate from it. I also mentor one junior engineer who joined last year, mostly through pairing on incident write-ups, since I think learning to reason about an incident calmly is as much the job as writing the original code.
answers.evidence_decision: About three years ago, the team wanted to introduce an event-sourcing model for claim status instead of our current mutable-row-plus-audit-log approach. I disagreed, because I'd measured our audit-log query patterns and found the team mostly needed point-in-time snapshots, which the current model already served in under 50ms, while a naive event-sourcing rebuild in a prototype I built took 300ms plus to reconstruct the same view. The team looked at that prototype and decided to keep the current model but add a proper snapshot table, a middle path I hadn't proposed myself. I built that snapshot table as agreed, and I didn't go back and quietly build the event-sourcing version on my own afterward, even though I still think it would have been technically interesting.
answers.own_contribution: In the state-machine incident, the guard-condition design and the fix were entirely mine -- I found the missing state check, wrote it, and wrote the regression test. What the team did was the fraud re-review of the four affected claims, which I didn't do myself, and the postmortem discussion on whether we needed a stricter escalation policy, which I ended up proposing. For a different example: on the connection-pool fix I described, tracing the thread dumps and deciding to split the reporting job's pool was entirely my own diagnosis, but another engineer wrote the actual pool-configuration change in our deployment manifests from my specification, since that repository wasn't one I had write access to at the time.
answers.java_recovery: After the sequence-number bug I described, I had to restore consistency for the six dropped payments. I scoped it with a query joining payment_attempts against the processor's settlement export for the same date range, which is how I found exactly six mismatches out of about 1,400 payments that week. I fixed each with a new payment_attempts row carrying a corrected sequence number rather than touching the rejected rows, then re-ran our nightly reconciliation job manually against just those six claim IDs to confirm the processor and our system agreed afterward. My first assumption, before I looked closely, was that all 60 rejected retries were affected, not just six; I only narrowed it down once I checked which of the 60 actually had a same-day amount change, which is what protected the other 54 from being real problems.
answers.java_perf_change: Our claim-search endpoint, used heavily by adjusters, sat at p99 of 1.1 seconds against a 400ms target. I measured with a profiler and found we were doing full-text search against Postgres with a trigram index for a field we mostly searched with a leading prefix. My first attempt was adding a Redis cache in front of it, which helped average case but did nothing for p99, since adjusters rarely searched the same claim twice. What worked was switching the index to match the prefix-search pattern we actually used, which took p99 to about 180ms. I kept the old index alongside the new one for a week to compare query plans before dropping it, in case some searches still needed the trigram behavior, which two of them did, so I kept both.
answers.rust_hands_on: In my claims-CSV tool, I got stuck trying to hold a reference to the current row while also building up a Vec of parsed rows to return, and the compiler kept rejecting it because the row reference borrowed from the file reader while I was also trying to own the parsed data long-term. I fixed it by having the parse function return owned String and f64 values immediately instead of holding onto references into the reader's buffer, accepting a small amount of copying I'd been trying to avoid. Separately, I fought a Send issue when I tried to share a running total across a couple of threads using a plain Rc, and switched to an Arc<Mutex<_>> once I understood Rc wasn't thread-safe, which felt obvious in hindsight but took me a confused evening to work out.
answers.rust_when_not: I'd hold off moving anything that's still actively changing shape, which in our world is the adjudication engine's state machine -- it's had three real behavior changes in the last year, and a rewrite target needs to sit still long enough to verify against. I haven't held back a full rewrite urge at work, since I've never had production Rust access to even propose one, but on my CSV tool I did hold back from rewriting the reporting-database write step into Rust just because I liked the language, once I noticed the Python script was already fast enough and well-tested; I decided that would have been rewriting for my own enjoyment, not for a real problem.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: During the same reconciliation cycle where I found the six dropped payments, I separately found a $940 mismatch across the month, all in one direction, unrelated to the sequence-number bug. I traced it to a batch of 8 claims where a late-arriving reinsurance adjustment posted after we'd already closed the month's settlement file, so our internal total moved but the file we'd sent didn't. I corrected it by including those 8 adjustments in the next month's file as their own line items rather than reopening the closed one, and flagged the timing gap to our reinsurance-ops contact so future late adjustments get held for the next cycle instead of landing mid-close. My first read was that it was a rounding issue, since $940 across a large batch looked small enough, and I only found the real cause once I checked timestamps against the file-close time.
answers.prod_data_verification: I've wanted to check a real balance against production more than once, mostly during the sequence-number incident, and what I actually did was take that week's payment_attempts and settlement export, strip claim-holder names and policy numbers, and run my reconciliation query against that masked copy in a scratch database instead of live. For anything I truly couldn't reproduce outside production, like confirming the guard-condition fix actually blocked the bad transition under real traffic timing, I used a read-only query against production that just checked whether any claim had entered the bad state since the fix, without touching or creating any records, and I posted what I was checking in our channel before running it.
